global.headline: IRAN WAR'S SEVENTH NIGHT: US HITS BRIDGES AND A PORT TOWER, IRAN STRIKES KUWAIT'S DESALINATION PLANT AND FIVE OTHER COUNTRIES, CASUALTIES TOP 38 DEAD
summary: CENTCOM struck Iran for a seventh consecutive night, hitting bridges in the southern port city of Bandar Khamir, additional energy sites, and collapsing a tower at a key Iranian port — part of a campaign the US says is intended to keep degrading Iranian military capability. Iran's Health Ministry said Friday that the strikes have killed 38 people (including three women and a child) and wounded more than 400, with 47 still hospitalised, since the current bombing campaign resumed in late June; Iranian state media (IRNA) separately said seven people died in Friday's Bandar Khamir bridge strikes alone.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard retaliated with missiles at six countries — Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Oman and Syria — the widest single-night spread of the conflict yet. Kuwait's Electricity Water and Renewable Energy Ministry said a desalination and power plant was hit, sparking a fire and damaging "a large number" of power-generation units; about 90% of Kuwait's drinking water comes from desalination. Qatar sounded shelter warnings twice as interceptors engaged an Iranian missile barrage, with falling debris wounding a child.

Oil climbed toward a one-month high — Brent crude up 0.9% to near $85/barrel, WTI up 1% to about $79.80 — with both benchmarks on track for roughly 12% weekly gains. Hormuz traffic fell to just eight confirmed crossings on Thursday, the lowest in three weeks per Kpler, with seven of the eight using the Iranian-controlled route rather than the US-backed corridor as shippers reassess security and insurance risk.
global.geopolitical: Widening Iranian retaliation to six countries in one night — and, for the first time, direct damage to a US-allied Gulf state's civilian water infrastructure — tests how much longer Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman and Jordan absorb collateral damage from a war none of them started, even as Washington shows no sign of slowing its own campaign.
global.socioeconomic: Oil near a one-month high and Hormuz crossings at a three-week low sustain the cost pressure already visible in Singapore's record COE premiums and Q3 electricity tariff, adding to the inflation pass-through MAS will need to weigh at its July policy meeting.

global.headline: ANDY BURNHAM CONFIRMED AS UK LABOUR LEADER, SET TO BECOME PRIME MINISTER MONDAY AS STARMER STEPS DOWN
summary: Andy Burnham, the left-leaning former Manchester mayor who returned to Westminster via a recent Makerfield by-election, was confirmed Friday as leader of Britain's governing Labour Party and will be appointed prime minister on Monday, succeeding Keir Starmer as Britain's seventh PM in a decade. In his acceptance speech, Burnham pledged to give people "hope back," criticising a political culture and economic model he said "simply doesn't work well enough for ordinary people," and vowed to unite the country against the challenge from the populist Reform UK party.
global.geopolitical: Resolves the open UK Labour leadership question tracked since nominations opened 9 July; Burnham inherits Britain's positions on NATO's €70B 2026 Ukraine pledge and the Vance-Israel rift over the Iran war without having campaigned on either.
global.socioeconomic: No direct Singapore impact, but a leadership change in a G7 economy arriving mid-way through an Iran-driven oil shock adds a fresh variable to how Europe manages energy-price pass-through, a dynamic Singapore's own cost-of-living data is already tracking.

global.headline: TRUMP DECLASSIFIES DOCUMENTS ALLEGING CHINA STOLE 220 MILLION US VOTER FILES IN 2020, OFFERS NO EVIDENCE VOTES WERE CHANGED; BEIJING REJECTS CLAIM
summary: In a primetime address Thursday, President Trump said he had declassified documents showing that, beginning with the 2020 election cycle, China carried out "the largest compromise of election data in history," illicitly acquiring 220 million US voter files, and repeated his long-standing claim that the 2020 election was "rigged." Over more than 20 minutes he did not present evidence that any votes or the election outcome were altered; independent review of the documents found nothing supporting that broader claim, and cited US intelligence assessments say China judged neither a Trump nor a Biden win worth the risk of getting caught meddling, preferring lower-profile economic and lobbying influence instead.

China's foreign ministry said it was "strongly dissatisfied" and rejected the allegation, declining to escalate further even as Xi Jinping continues planning a state visit to Washington. Separately, the Trump administration's Homeland Security chief threatened unspecified action against state election officials, and the speech coincided with a renewed push for the SAVE America Act's citizenship-verification provisions ahead of the midterms.
global.geopolitical: Opens a new US-China friction point even as Trump pursues a deeper personal bond with Xi, and feeds directly into the SAVE Act push already entangled with the House GOP's $95bn Iran-war budget fight.
global.socioeconomic: Muted Chinese market reaction suggests Beijing is avoiding a fight; no direct Singapore exposure, though it adds to the broader US-China unpredictability that Singapore's trade-dependent economy continues to navigate.

global.headline: TRUMP THREATENS TO ADD WILDFIRE-SMOKE COSTS TO CANADA TARIFFS AS 896 BLAZES BLANKET 18 US STATES IN HAZARDOUS AIR
summary: President Trump said Friday he is holding Canada responsible for wildfire smoke drifting into the US Midwest and Northeast and would add "the cost of this pollution" onto tariffs Canada already pays, saying he would call PM Mark Carney directly and accusing Ottawa of failing to address the fires' causes. Canadian officials are fighting 896 active wildfires nationwide; more than 100 million people across 18 US states and Washington DC remain under air-quality alerts, with "hazardous" readings in Michigan and "very unhealthy" conditions in Wisconsin and Minnesota.
global.geopolitical: Escalates a climate-driven irritant into a fresh trade threat against Canada, layering atop the existing tariff relationship and testing Carney's position that wildfire response is a shared US-Canada responsibility rather than a one-sided failure.
global.socioeconomic: No direct Singapore exposure to this bilateral dispute, but it's a reminder that US tariff-escalation risk remains live even away from the Iran-driven headlines dominating global trade anxiety this week.

global.headline: UKRAINE'S FEDOROV OUSTER SPARKS WIDENING PROTESTS AND TALK OF A ZELENSKY RIVAL, AS SOLDIERS AND VETERANS DEMAND HIS REINSTATEMENT
summary: Protests against President Zelensky's dismissal of Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov grew through Thursday into Friday, with thousands rallying outside the President's Office in Kyiv and in other cities demanding parliament reinstate him. Soldiers, veterans and civil-society figures argue Ukraine is losing one of its most effective wartime officials — credited with jamming Russian drone/Starlink use and modernising procurement — over what Zelensky described only as unresolved friction with commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi. Analysts are now openly asking whether Zelensky, in removing his most popular minister, has inadvertently created a political rival.
global.geopolitical: A rare, sustained domestic political crisis inside wartime Ukraine, arriving in the same reshuffle that installed new PM Serhii Koretskyi; watch whether it destabilises the drone/Starlink-denial programmes Fedorov built or imposes lasting political costs on Zelensky.
global.socioeconomic: None material for Singapore directly; continued churn in Kyiv's wartime cabinet keeps uncertainty elevated for European aid and defence planning alongside the Iran-driven energy shock.

singapore.headline: CHIEF JUSTICE SUNDARESH MENON TO RETIRE FEBRUARY 2027 AFTER 14 YEARS; JUSTICE SUSHIL NAIR NAMED SINGAPORE'S 5TH CHIEF JUSTICE
summary: The Prime Minister's Office announced Friday that Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon will retire on 26 February 2027, having served more than 14 years in the role. Justice Sushil Sukumaran Nair, currently a Justice of the Court of Appeal, has been appointed to succeed him with effect from that date. Justice Nair had a 35-year legal career — including as Deputy CEO of Drew & Napier and head of its corporate restructuring and workouts practice — before joining the Bench as Judicial Commissioner in April 2025 and being elevated to the Court of Appeal on 15 June 2026.
singapore.geopolitical: None material — a domestic judicial succession, though CJ Menon's tenure included chairing international judicial bodies that raised Singapore's profile in global commercial-dispute resolution.
singapore.socioeconomic: A smooth succession announced more than seven months ahead signals continuity in Singapore's judiciary and legal-hub positioning, the same institutional-stability narrative underpinning cases like the Hin Leong-Deloitte litigation below.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE'S APEX COURT STRIKES OUT HIN LEONG LIQUIDATORS' US$2.6B CLAIM AGAINST DELOITTE, CALLING IT 'TOO REMOTE'
summary: Singapore's Court of Appeal has struck out the largest of several claims brought by collapsed oil trader Hin Leong's liquidators against auditor Deloitte, which sought to hold the firm liable for US$2.6 billion (about S$3.4 billion) in trading losses racked up between 2015 and 2020. The court found the losses stemmed not from the financing Hin Leong obtained but from how the Lim family's controlling shareholders subsequently used the borrowed money — too remote from Deloitte's audit work to sustain a claim — rejecting the liquidators' argument as one that "cuts no ice." Two smaller claims against Deloitte remain live: US$90 million (about S$118 million) over dividends the liquidators say were wrongfully declared by the Lim family in 2017-2018, and US$612,000 (about S$800,000) in disputed audit fees.
singapore.geopolitical: None material — a domestic apex-court commercial ruling, though it will be closely read by auditors and litigation funders globally given Hin Leong's status as one of the largest corporate collapses in Singapore's history.
singapore.socioeconomic: Striking out the headline US$2.6b claim sharply cuts Deloitte's exposure and the potential recovery for Hin Leong's creditors, a major data point in a long-running case testing how far Singapore courts will extend auditor liability for a client's own trading decisions.

singapore.headline: GOVTECH RETRENCHES 93 STAFF IN FIRST PHASE OF TWO-YEAR SHIFT AWAY FROM VENDOR-DELIVERED PROJECTS
summary: Singapore's Government Technology Agency has retrenched 93 officers in the first phase of a restructuring set to affect 7-9% of its workforce over the next two years, as it shifts from a vendor-delivered project model to directly owning and running government digital products and platforms on an ongoing basis. Of 305 officers assessed in this phase — covering six forward-deployed teams embedded in other agencies plus one central function — 102 were retained and 110 placed into reskilling apprenticeships, alongside the 93 retrenched. GovTech said it will hire more software engineers, product managers, designers, data specialists, cybersecurity experts and platform engineers under the new model; NTUC's e2i has deployed on-site career coaches, with close to 30 companies offering 300+ tech vacancies and a curated career fair set for 4 August. The Public Service Division said the exercise is specific to GovTech, not part of a broader public-service-wide restructuring.
singapore.socioeconomic: A sizeable public-sector retrenchment lands alongside Q1 2026's already-elevated 3,830 retrenchments (highest since Q3 2023), adding a white-collar tech-sector data point to Singapore's job-security narrative even as the agency signals continued hiring demand in the same skill areas it is cutting from.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE CANCELS WORK PERMITS OF TWO BANGLADESHI NATIONALS OVER EXTREMIST SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS, REPATRIATES THEM
summary: Singapore's Internal Security Department investigated and repatriated two Bangladeshi work-permit holders, Tayani Md Risad, 25, and Islam Sahedul, 37, after separately finding extremist and divisive social-media activity: Risad had expressed support for radical Islamist writer Shafiur Rahman Farabi, who has incited violence against secular and atheist bloggers, while Sahedul posted inflammatory content about the Israel-Iran conflict and called Muslims who reject governance under Islamic law "infidels." ISD said neither man showed intent to conduct attacks or engage in terrorism in Singapore, but their views were "inimical to Singapore's multiracial and multi-religious society."
singapore.geopolitical: Continues Singapore's pattern (the 69-person moneylending crackdown 9 Jul, earlier ISA arrests of 27 radicalised Bangladeshi nationals) of pre-emptive administrative action against foreign workers' online extremism, a lower bar than the Internal Security Act detentions used for more serious cases.
singapore.socioeconomic: Reinforces scrutiny of the large Bangladeshi work-permit-holder population at a time when Singapore is separately weighing foreign-workforce policy amid COE and cost-of-living pressures.

singapore.headline: 100 ARRESTED IN ISLANDWIDE ANTI-DRUG OPERATION ACROSS EIGHT ESTATES
summary: The Central Narcotics Bureau arrested 100 suspected drug offenders in an islandwide operation spanning Boon Lay, Ghim Moh, Jurong, Kallang, Tampines, Tengah, Toa Payoh and Woodlands between 12-17 July, seizing about 859g of cannabis, 120g of heroin, 85g of Ice, 3g of Ecstasy tablets and two Erimin-5 tablets — enough, CNB said, to have fed 228 abusers' addictions for a week. One case involved a 28-year-old Singaporean man arrested on 14 July on suspected trafficking charges.
singapore.socioeconomic: None material beyond standing enforcement activity — a routine but sizeable operation consistent with Singapore's ongoing anti-drug enforcement posture.

word.definition: The condition or habit of being untruthful; a lie or falsehood, especially one told persistently or deliberately.
word.etymology: From Latin mendax ("lying, false, deceptive"), related to mendum ("fault, blemish, error"); entered English in the 17th century via the adjective "mendacious."
word.example: Independent review of Trump's newly declassified documents found no evidence backing his repeated claim that the 2020 election was stolen — highlighting real Chinese data theft doesn't erase the mendacity of the larger 'rigged election' narrative built around it.
